title: OCD 1 — Test
src: Developmental diseases of oral & para-oral structures

mcqs.q: “Congenital” means a condition that is:
opts: Existing at or dating from birth
Caused only by a DNA mutation
mcqs.explain: Congenital = present at / dating from birth; it is not necessarily genetic.

mcqs.q: A genetic disorder is one that results from:
mcqs.explain: A genetic disorder occurs as a result of a mutation to DNA; a developmental disorder is marked by delayed development/impaired function.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of a MUTAGENIC (environmental) cause of developmental disturbance?
mcqs.explain: Mutagenesis includes infections (rubella, influenza), radiation, hormones, nutrition, drugs and maternal disease; inheritance is the separate genetic category.

mcqs.q: Developmental diseases are classified by TIME into:
mcqs.explain: By time: prenatal (1st–3rd trimester) and postnatal (neonatal → adolescence). Intrinsic/extrinsic is the etiologic classification.

mcqs.q: Cleft palate occurs in approximately how many live births?
mcqs.explain: Cleft palate occurs in about 1 in 700 live births worldwide, frequently together with cleft lip.

mcqs.q: The multifactorial threshold (Bixler) hypothesis states that a cleft occurs when:
opts: The total genetic liability passes a threshold level
A single dominant gene is inherited
The fetus is exposed to one teratogen
mcqs.explain: When the combined genetic liability of an individual exceeds the threshold for expression, a cleft results.

mcqs.q: The surgical “rule of three 10s” for cleft lip repair refers to:
opts: 10 lb weight, 10 g/L hemoglobin, 10 weeks of age
mcqs.explain: The classic readiness criteria are about 10 lb body weight, hemoglobin ~10, and age ~10 weeks.

mcqs.q: Pierre Robin sequence is characterised by a small jaw with:
opts: The tongue pushed into the pharynx and airway obstruction
A cleft of the upper lip only
mcqs.explain: Pierre Robin: micrognathia → the tongue is displaced posteriorly into the pharynx, causing airway obstruction.

mcqs.q: The earliest sign of hemifacial atrophy is:
opts: A cleft or furrow in the midline of the face
mcqs.explain: Hemifacial (progressive) atrophy first shows a cleft/furrow in the facial midline; Parry-Romberg syndrome is the associated condition.

mcqs.q: Hemifacial atrophy associated with contralateral Jacksonian epilepsy and trigeminal neuralgia is called:
mcqs.explain: Parry-Romberg syndrome combines progressive hemifacial atrophy with neurologic and ocular changes.

mcqs.q: When TWO adjacent tooth germs unite, producing one less tooth in the arch, the anomaly is:
mcqs.explain: Fusion = union of two germs (one fewer tooth). Gemination = one germ splits (normal count). Concrescence = union by cementum only.

mcqs.q: Gemination differs from fusion in that the tooth count is:
mcqs.explain: In gemination a single germ attempts to divide, so the number of teeth remains normal.

mcqs.q: Amelogenesis imperfecta is a developmental disturbance of tooth:
mcqs.explain: Amelogenesis imperfecta affects enamel structure; dentinogenesis imperfecta and dentin dysplasia affect dentin.

mcqs.q: Anodontia is a developmental disturbance of tooth:
mcqs.explain: Anodontia = missing teeth (number); supernumerary = extra teeth.

mcqs.q: This image shows an enlarged, protruding tongue. The condition is:
mcqs.explain: Macroglossia = an abnormally large tongue, often presenting as a protruding tongue with stridor, drooling and speech difficulty.

mcqs.q: Which syndrome is a recognised cause of macroglossia?
mcqs.explain: Macroglossia is linked to Down, Hunter and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndromes, and to amyloidosis, hypothyroidism and acromegaly.

mcqs.q: Ankyloglossia (tongue-tie) is due to:
opts: A short, tight lingual frenulum restricting tongue movement
mcqs.explain: Ankyloglossia is an unusually short/thick/tight lingual frenulum that tethers the tongue and may interfere with feeding and speech.

mcqs.q: This tongue shows deep grooves on the dorsum. The condition is:
mcqs.explain: A fissured tongue (lingua plicata) shows furrows 2–6 mm deep; food entrapment can cause halitosis and glossitis.

mcqs.q: Approximately what proportion of patients with a lingual (ectopic) thyroid are hypothyroid?
mcqs.explain: Around 70% of patients with ectopic (lingual) thyroid tissue are hypothyroid; it results from failed descent of the thyroid.

mcqs.q: This intraoral image shows ectopic tissue at the base of the tongue. It is a:
mcqs.explain: A lingual thyroid is a mass of ectopic thyroid tissue at the tongue base from an embryologic failure of descent.

mcqs.q: Lingual varicosities are clinically:
opts: Harmless degenerative venous changes of the ventral tongue
mcqs.explain: They are tortuous blue/purple elevations on the ventrolateral tongue, of no clinical consequence and not prone to rupture.

mcqs.q: The colour of a “hairy tongue” is produced mainly by:
opts: Elongated filiform papillae trapping pigment-producing organisms
mcqs.explain: Hairy tongue = elongated filiform papillae/keratin in which bacteria and yeast accumulate, giving brown/black/green discolouration.

mcqs.q: Lower-lip pits occurring together with cleft lip/palate define:
mcqs.explain: The association of lower-lip pits with cleft lip and/or palate is van der Woude syndrome.

mcqs.q: This image illustrates pits of the lower lip. They represent:
opts: Failure of union of the embryonic lateral sulci of the lip
mcqs.explain: Lip pits arise from notching/failure of complete union of the embryonic lateral sulci of the lip; mucus may exude from the base.

mcqs.q: A congenital double lip is classically part of:
opts: Ascher syndrome (with blepharochalasis and thyroid enlargement)
mcqs.explain: Congenital double lip is associated with Ascher syndrome — double lip + blepharochalasis (droopy eyelids) + thyroid enlargement.

mcqs.q: Fordyce granules are histologically collections of:
mcqs.explain: Fordyce granules are ectopic sebaceous glands appearing as small yellow spots, usually on the buccal mucosa; they need no treatment.

mcqs.q: Leukoedema is best regarded as:
opts: A variant of normal mucosa requiring no treatment
mcqs.explain: Leukoedema is a filmy grayish-white change correlated with tobacco use; it is a normal variant and needs no treatment.

mcqs.q: This image shows a filmy grayish-white change of the buccal mucosa that is a normal variant. It is:
mcqs.explain: Leukoedema is an opalescent/grayish-white wrinkled buccal mucosa, a benign variant of normal closely linked to smoking.

mcqs.q: Gingival fibromatosis is in most reported cases:
mcqs.explain: Most cases are hereditary, transmitted through a dominant autosomal gene; treatment is surgical removal of excess tissue.

mcqs.q: This radiograph shows a well-defined radiolucency near the angle of the mandible, found incidentally. It is:
mcqs.explain: Stafne's (static) bone defect is a benign developmental bony depression — often submandibular gland tissue — found incidentally on radiograph; no surgery is needed.

saqs.a: Congenital = existing at/dating from birth. Developmental disorder = delayed development or impaired function (communication, learning, behaviour). Genetic disorder = results from a mutation to DNA.

saqs.q: List the two broad categories of causes of developmental disturbances, with examples.
saqs.a: A. Mutagenesis (environmental): infections (rubella/influenza), physical injury/radiation, hormones, nutritional deficiency, drugs (tetracyclines, thalidomide), maternal disease. B. Genetic inheritance: transmitted gene mutations.
Fusion = union of two tooth germs → one fewer tooth in the arch. Gemination = a single germ tries to split → tooth count remains normal.
Syndromes (Down, Beckwith-Wiedemann, Hunter); acquired (amyloidosis, hypothyroidism, acromegaly); neoplasms (lymphangioma, hemangioma, lymphoma).

saqs.q: What is a lingual thyroid and why is thyroid status important?
saqs.a: Ectopic thyroid tissue at the base of the tongue from failed embryologic descent. It matters because about 70% of patients are hypothyroid, and it may cause dysphagia/dysphonia or airway obstruction.

saqs.q: Name the syndromes associated with (a) lower-lip pits + cleft and (b) double lip.
saqs.a: (a) van der Woude syndrome (lip pits + cleft lip/palate). (b) Ascher syndrome (double lip + blepharochalasis + thyroid enlargement).
